title: Boring-NixOS
text:
Boring NixOS
From Zero to Production — Reproducible Systems at Scale
A linear guide to writing Nix and managing NixOS systems the way they actually work in production: deterministic, immutable, and delightfully boring.
Clarity beats cleverness. Explicit dependencies beat ambient runtime state. The boring default is the configuration that builds identically on your laptop, your CI pipeline, and your production bare-metal cluster six months from now.

title: Boring-NixOS
text:
Who this is for

Engineers, platform architects, and SREs who are exhausted by “works on my machine” drift and irreproducible production outages.
Developers who want clean, instant development environments without container overhead or dependency hell.
Teams migrating from ad-hoc configuration management (Ansible, bash scripts, Docker Desktop) to pure declarative infrastructure.

You do not need prior Nix or NixOS experience. You only need a terminal, a standard text editor, and a commitment to reproducibility.

title: Boring-NixOS
text:
What “boring” means here
Nix is a purely functional package manager and domain-specific configuration language. When used with discipline, Nix eliminates entire categories of operational failure: broken library symlinks, partial OS upgrades, conflicting glibc versions, and undocumented server state.
When abused, Nix can become an unreadable puzzle of undocumented overlays and over-engineered macros.
Boring NixOS teaches the disciplined default: clean derivation structures, readable Nix expressions, explicit pinned inputs, and maintainable NixOS modules that scale from a single desktop to fleet infrastructure.

title: Boring-NixOS
text:
How examples work
Every code listing is a self-contained, complete expression or file: - # default.nix - # shell.nix - # flake.nix - # configuration.nix
No fragmented snippets or guessing missing imports. You can copy the listing directly into your file, run the indicated command, and see the exact expected output.

title: Nix Fundamentals — How It Actually Works
text:
Nix Fundamentals — How It Actually Works
The traditional operating system model is mutable: packages overwrite shared files in /usr/lib and /usr/bin, creating unpredictable state and silent breakage. The boring default of Nix is: every package is an immutable, content-addressed path under /nix/store, determined strictly by cryptographic hashes of its inputs.

title: Nix Fundamentals — How It Actually Works
text:
Mental model
In traditional package managers (apt, dnf, brew), installing package A can silently upgrade library B, breaking package C that depended on the old version of B. This is the root cause of dependency rot and non-reproducible environments.
Nix solves this by treating software installations like a pure functional evaluation:

The Nix Store (/nix/store): Every artifact lives in an isolated directory whose path includes a cryptographic hash, such as /nix/store/s69al102...-ripgrep-14.1.0.
Deterministic Hashes: The hash is computed from all inputs that produce the package: source code, compiler flags, dependencies, and build scripts. If any dependency changes by a single bit, the output path changes.
No Ambient State: Builds run inside isolated sandboxes without access to the host network or root filesystem. A program cannot inadvertently link against whatever compiler happened to be installed in /usr/bin.
Symlink Trees: Environments and user profiles are symlink trees pointing to specific /nix/store paths. Upgrading or switching environments simply means swapping a symlink.
Garbage Collection: Deleting a package removes the symlink from your profile. The underlying store paths remain safely until nix-collect-garbage cleans unreferenced store entries.

/nix/store/
├── a1b2c3d4...-glibc-2.39/
├── f9e8d7c6...-ripgrep-14.1.0/  -> references glibc-2.39
└── b7a6c5d4...-ripgrep-14.0.0/  -> references older glibc
Both versions coexist on the same disk without collision or conflict.

title: Nix Fundamentals — How It Actually Works
text:
Worked examples

Case 1: Inspecting the Nix Store
Check where an installed utility actually lives on disk.
Run:
which rg
Output:
/nix/store/z1k947f6y788sfaivs931h26hsvb3506-ripgrep-14.1.0/bin/rg
Notice that the binary does not reside in /usr/bin/rg. It is an immutable, isolated path.


Case 2: Querying Exact Runtime Dependencies
Inspect the dependency graph of an executable using nix-store -q --references.
Run:
nix-store -q --references $(which rg)
Output:
/nix/store/7r44p12l4b72j9m9l09k96yghz02f8n7-glibc-2.39
/nix/store/z1k947f6y788sfaivs931h26hsvb3506-ripgrep-14.1.0
Every library needed by rg is explicitly recorded. There are no undeclared ambient dependencies.


Case 3: Evaluating a Pure Expression
Save as hello.nix. A minimal Nix expression that defines a string value.
# hello.nix
let
  greeting = "Hello, reproducible world!";
in
greeting
Run:
nix-instantiate --eval hello.nix
Output:
"Hello, reproducible world!"
Nix is an expression language. Evaluating an expression computes a deterministic value.


Case 4: Creating a Trivially Reproducible Derivation
Save as greeting.nix. A complete self-contained derivation using the built-in derivation primitive.
# greeting.nix
derivation {
  name = "desk-greeting";
  system = builtins.currentSystem;
  builder = "/bin/sh";
  args = [
    "-c"
    "echo 'Desk system operational' > $out"
  ];
}
Run:
nix-build greeting.nix
Output:
these 1 derivations will be built:
  /nix/store/m6a1p...-desk-greeting.drv
building '/nix/store/m6a1p...-desk-greeting.drv'...
/nix/store/k3b29...-desk-greeting
Inspect the generated output:
cat result
Output:
Desk system operational
result is a local symlink pointing directly into /nix/store.


Case 5: Garbage Collection and Roots
Remove the symlink and run garbage collection.
Run:
rm result
nix-collect-garbage
Output:
finding garbage collector roots...
deleting garbage...
deleting '/nix/store/k3b29...-desk-greeting'
1 store paths deleted, 0.00 MiB freed
Because no active symlink (garbage collector root) references desk-greeting, the store reclaims the space.

title: Nix Fundamentals — How It Actually Works
text:
The trap
Save as bad_build.sh. Trying to run conventional make install or pip install globally directly writes into system directories, creating untracked file clutter.
# bad_build.sh
# Anti-pattern: mutating shared system state
sudo cp myapp /usr/local/bin/myapp
When /usr/local/bin/myapp breaks after an OS update, no tool knows which dependencies it relied upon or how to roll it back.
The fix: Define software as a Nix derivation or shell environment. Every file remains tracked, sandboxed, and reversible.

title: Nix Fundamentals — How It Actually Works
text:
The boring rule

All binaries and libraries belong in /nix/store, never in mutable system paths.
Depend on explicit store paths, never on whatever happens to be on $PATH.
Use nix-store -q --tree to inspect dependency chains.
Run nix-collect-garbage -d periodically to remove stale generations and unreferenced store paths.

title: Nix Fundamentals — How It Actually Works
text:
Try this

Run nix-store -q --tree $(which nix) and observe the complete tree of dependencies required by the Nix binary itself.
In greeting.nix, modify the greeting text to 'Front desk open' and re-run nix-build. Note how the hash in the resulting /nix/store path changes.
Check your current garbage collector roots using nix-store --gc --print-roots.

title: The Nix Language — From Basics to Advanced Patterns
text:
The Nix Language — From Basics to Advanced Patterns
Nix is not a general-purpose programming language; it is a pure, lazy, functional configuration language. The boring default is: write explicit attribute sets with clear argument destructuring, keep expressions small, and let laziness compute only what is actually built.

title: The Nix Language — From Basics to Advanced Patterns
text:
Mental model
Nix has six primary primitive types (integers, floats, booleans, strings, paths, and null) plus lists and attribute sets.

Pure: Functions have no side effects. A function called with the same inputs always produces identical output.
Lazy: Values are only evaluated when their result is needed. You can define infinite lists or huge attribute sets without paying a performance penalty until a specific key is accessed.
Attribute Sets ({ a = 1; b = 2; }): The primary dictionary/object construct.
Functions (x: x + 1): All functions take exactly one argument. Multi-argument functions are curried (x: y: x + y) or accept an attribute set ({ x, y }: x + y).
Let-In (let ... in ...): Defines local variables scoped strictly within the expression following in.

title: The Nix Language — From Basics to Advanced Patterns
The Nix Language — From Basics to Advanced Patterns
The Nix Language — From Basics to Advanced Patterns
text:
The boring rule

Prefer explicit let ... in blocks over rec attribute sets.
Use attribute set destructuring { pkgs, lib, ... }: for clean component interfaces.
Always use ? default when an option has a sane default value.
Keep .nix files small and single-purpose; compose them with import.
Rely on laziness: define full configurations without worrying about premature evaluation.

title: The Nix Language — From Basics to Advanced Patterns
text:
Try this

In functions.nix, add an optional boolean argument ssl ? true and include "https" or "http" in the service URL based on its value.
In collections.nix, write a function that sums all numbers in the list.
Create a helper file math.nix exporting add and multiply, and call it from a new app.nix.

title: Reproducible Development Environments
text:
Reproducible Development Environments
Development environment drift is the single most common source of onboarding friction and subtle bugs across software teams. The boring default is: a single flake.nix or shell.nix checked into the repository root that provisions exact, pinned compilers, tools, and linters instantly without VM overhead.

title: Reproducible Development Environments
text:
Mental model
Teams traditionally manage development environments with one of three flawed approaches: - Global system packages: “Install Go with brew and Python with apt” leads to subtle version mismatches across developer laptops. - Version managers (asdf, pyenv, nvm): Better, but only manage language runtimes. They fail to manage underlying C libraries, headers, pkg-config, or system tools like cmake and jq. - Heavy Docker containers (Docker Desktop): Slow to start, consume excessive memory/CPU, and introduce file permission headaches between container and host filesystems.
A Nix devShell provides an instant ephemeral shell environment where the exact toolchain and dependencies are injected directly into your $PATH and library flags without running a virtual machine or container daemon.
When you exit the shell, your system remains pristine.
Host OS (Linux / macOS)
  └── nix develop
        ├── Injects exact Go 1.27, Node 22, Terraform, and libpq
        ├── Sets $PKG_CONFIG_PATH and compiler flags
        └── Exiting drops back to your normal pristine host environment

title: Reproducible Development Environments
Reproducible Development Environments
text:
The trap
Save as docker_drift.txt. Relying on bulky Docker containers for routine local development causes synchronization issues and high overhead.
# Anti-pattern: Running basic compilers inside fat containers
docker run -v $(pwd):/app -it ubuntu:latest bash -c "apt-get update && apt-get install -y gcc"
Problems: - 10x slower file I/O on macOS/Windows host mounts. - Host IDE cannot easily see language servers (gopls, pyright) running inside the container. - High RAM consumption compared to native execution.
The fix: Use Nix devShell for native host performance, direct editor integration, and zero container overhead.

title: Reproducible Development Environments
text:
The boring rule

Commit a flake.nix and flake.lock at the root of every shared repository.
Use pkgs.mkShell with explicit packages lists.
Set shared environment variables (CGO_ENABLED, PGDATABASE) in the shell definition.
Pair with direnv and use flake for zero-click environment activation.
Never force developers to install language runtimes globally on their workstations.

title: Reproducible Development Environments
text:
Try this

In flake.nix, add pkgs.htop to the packages list and run nix develop --command htop to verify on-demand binary injection.
Add a shellHook script that prints an ASCII banner when entering the shell.
Test that variables exported in shell.nix vanish as soon as you exit the nix-shell.
